obtained.how: agency copy: the Michigan DNR Fisheries Division library PDF of Institute for Fisheries Research Report 1106 (typescript scan with a text layer, 9 pages); Table 1 read on the page image

bibliography.note: Report No. 1106, dated March 24, 1947, Institute for Fisheries Research (Michigan Department of Conservation with the University of Michigan), by Stanley J. Lievense; title as cited

claims.claim: the inlet creek of Big Portage Lake is 400 m long, 2.7 m wide and 0.46 m deep
claims.source_value: the creek's stretch between the lake and an artificial trout pond is one-fourth mile (≈ 400 m); 9 ft (2.7 m) wide and 1.5 ft (0.46 m) deep is its LOWER section, where the weir stood ~150 yd (137 m) above the lake; the upper section below the pond is ~4 ft (1.2 m) wide and 1–3 ft (0.3–0.9 m) deep. Spring-fed, moderately swift, summer flow ~2 cfs (~0.06 m³/s), marl and peat bottom with a thin sand layer and occasional rubble and gravel
claims.quote: approximately 9 feet wide and 1-1/2 feet deep in the lower section
claims.note: minor: the width and depth are the lower section's, not the creek's; the pools where sunfish summered lie in a creek 1–3 ft deep

claims.location: p. 1 (PDF p. 1) and pp. 2–3 (PDF pp. 2–3); Table 1 (PDF p. 9)
claims.quote: It was installed on March 15 and checked for the first time
claims.conditions: checked daily 15 March–17 June 1946 (open on 16–17 May in high water); trap with 1/2-inch wire cones, so small fish passed through

claims.claim: moving up from the lake: 1,786 bluegill, 654 pumpkinseed, 299 yellow and 193 black bullheads
claims.location: Table 1, upstream migrants, totals (PDF p. 9; read on the page image)
claims.quote: Pumpkinseed … 654; Bluegill … 1,786; Yellow bullhead … 299; Black bullhead … 193
claims.conditions: trap counts, 16 March–17 June 1946; downstream over the same period: 163 pumpkinseed, 400 bluegill, 52 yellow and 22 black bullheads

claims.claim: moving up from the lake: 113 white suckers, 49 mud pickerel, 40 largemouth and 9 yellow perch
claims.location: Table 1, upstream migrants, totals (PDF p. 9; read on the page image)
claims.quote: Common sucker … 113; Mud pickerel … 49; Largemouth bass … 40; Yellow perch 9
claims.conditions: 'common sucker (Catostomus c. commersonnii)' = white sucker; also 120 chub suckers, 62 rock bass, 11 longear sunfish, 9 black crappie up

claims.claim: the centrarchids' 'migration was not for the purpose of spawning'
claims.source_value: said of the bluegills and (pumpkinseed) sunfish only, from their small size (most bluegills 2–4.5 in.) and the creek's habitat; nothing is said of the 40 largemouth bass (3–13 in., most ~9 in.), which came up from 21 April when the water reached 50 °F
claims.quote: The small size of the bluegills and sunfish and the type of habitat
claims.note: write 'the bluegills' and pumpkinseeds' migration …' instead of 'the centrarchids''

claims.claim: 'many bluegills and sunfish were observed in several of the larger pools of the creek throughout the summer'
claims.quote: Many bluegills and sunfish were observed in several of the larger pools
claims.conditions: many upstream centrarchids had not returned by 17 June; the largest downstream movement came in the last weeks, so 'many returned to the lake after the trap was removed'

claims.claim: the share of pumpkinseed that move into the brook's pools for the summer (0.3) — Lievense 1947 and the angler
claims.note: Lievense gives weir counts, not a share: there is no estimate of the lake's pumpkinseed population. Pumpkinseed were taken every week (654 up, 163 down by 17 June), and 'many' bluegills and sunfish stayed in the larger pools all summer. Cite Lievense for the behaviour; the 0.3 is the project's (or the angler's) estimate and should be labelled so

notes: Other context for the rewrite: the creek is the lake's INLET, below an artificial trout pond, not an outlet or a connecting stream between two lakes; the weir's purpose was to track trout escaping the pond. Bullheads ran mostly in the last half of March (sizes 2–10 in. yellow, 3–7 in. black), judged not to be spawning; the white suckers made a definite spawning run (97 of 113 mature, mid-April to early May, water 52–55 °F), and only 14 returned, all bruised and fungused.
